en: [Opening of the *Ślokavārttika*] || May there be no obstacle! ||
Among humans, the brahmin is supreme; among luminous bodies, the sun is supreme; and among all limbs of the body, the head is supreme; likewise, among all dharmas, truth is supreme. (1)

[Chapter 1] Kaliṅanya: Herein is the Dharma for those who desire to know the distinctions of birth. Among humans, there is none superior to the Brāhmaṇa. A Brāhmaṇa is one who maintains the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). There are three types of him. They are as follows: there is the *śukla-brahmacārī* (white celibate), the *śavala-brahmacārī* (speckled celibate), and the *kṛṣṇa-brahmacārī* (black celibate). He is called a Brāhmaṇa; he is indeed superior to the human birth. He is called a *śukla-brahmacārī*. He does not emit semen; he does not ejaculate nor does he discharge it. Even when he has reached old age, he still does not ejaculate semen. Such is the one called a *brahmacārī*, provided he is a *śukla-brahmacārī*. He is called a *śavala-brahmacārī*. He emits semen frequently, yet does not ejaculate further. However, if he is overcome by the death of his wife, he does not ejaculate further and further until he reaches his own death. Even then, he does not ejaculate semen. Such is the *brahmacārī* who is a *śavala-brahmacārī*. He is called a *kṛṣṇa-brahmacārī*. He emits semen four times a day, yet does not ejaculate further. Who in the world could provide an illustration of such a thing? It is the Lord Rudra; he has four goddesses as his consorts. What are the names of these goddesses? Umā, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, and Durgā. These are the four sisters, the goddesses, who are taken as wives by the *kṛṣṇa-brahmacārī*. Nevertheless, he must know the proper time and place for union with women. Such is the sequence of the various types of *brahmacārīs*.
What indeed is fire? There is no fire like that of the venerable sun; it is the preeminent fire in the world.
Furthermore, there is no part of the entire body that is not like the head in its essential nature.
Such is this Dharma; there is nothing superior to it, for it is the most excellent in the world.
On a lunar day, a gift is tenfold; on an eclipse, it is a hundredfold;
when the sun has entered Virgo, it is a thousandfold; and at the end of the eon, it is infinite.

[Śloka 02j] Regarding the Kali age: when it is full, at that time a virtuous person who bestows meritorious gifts returns as one in ten parts of the Lord. However, during a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, a virtuous person who bestows meritorious gifts returns as one in a hundred parts of the Lord. Furthermore, at the time of the arrival of a daughter (kanyāgata), a virtuous person who bestows meritorious gifts returns as one in a thousand parts of the Lord. Moreover, at the time of the end of the eon (yugāntakāla), a virtuous person who bestows those meritorious gifts returns as one part that cannot be entered by the Lord; this is because of the intensity of the primary elements of that person.
A gift given to one who is not a brāhmaṇa is equal; to those who are mere nominal brāhmaṇas it is twofold;
to a learned brāhmaṇa it is a thousandfold; and to one who has mastered the Vedas it is infinite.

[Kaliṅganyā: "It is good that you have offered this gift of merit (*puṇyadāna*). If one gives a gift to an ordinary person, it does not reach a *brāhmaṇa*, nor does it reach a wise man (*paṇḍita*), nor is there any ascetic merit (*tapas*) in it; yet, if one offers a gift of merit, that which is given returns singlefold from the Lord (*bhaṭāra*). Furthermore, if one gives a gift to a *brāhmaṇa*, that gift given by a virtuous person (*sādhujana*) returns twofold. Moreover, if that *brāhmaṇa* gives a gift to a virtuous person, that which is given returns sevenfold from the Lord. Furthermore, if that *brāhmaṇa* is a master of the Vedas (*vedapāraga*) and gives a gift to a virtuous person, that gift returns manifold and is not exhausted by the Lord. A *brāhmaṇa* who is a master of the Vedas is a *brāhmaṇa* who knows the *veda-śāstra* completely."
Even if that gift is performed accompanied by only a slight degree of faith,
one obtains a great fruit, like the seed of a nyagrodha sprout.

[Kaliṅanya: This is the virtuous person (*sādhujana*), who bestows meritorious gifts (*puṇyadāna*). Even if the gift is small, the merit of that giving brings happiness to the mind of the giver. The reason for this is the purity of the heart of the one who gives the gift. "Purity" means sincerity. The giver of the gift shall obtain that fruit. How is it compared? It is like a single seed of rice: at the end, it sprouts; when it is cultivated, at the end there is no doubt that it will yield a harvest. It is capable of being the sustenance for a person, whether in an inferior, middling, or superior birth. Such is the meritorious gift, even if small, provided the mind is sincere. Its fruit will flourish by the grace of the Lord (*bhaṭāra*).
Indeed, even an infinite gift given by donors when mixed with anger will surely result in ashes,
just as the addition of grass to a fire inevitably leads to its extinction.

[Kaliṅga: "There is indeed a gift, but it does not reach the wise man to whom it was intended to be increased. Although the Brāhmaṇa who received it gave that gift away, all the value of that gift vanished; yet he himself became full of anger. Anger is like a fire that burns the mouth, clings to the throat, sears the heart, and consumes the body. Such is the result of his giving; its essence is ruined. It is not true merit, for it is merely the loss of one's wealth and possessions. He says, 'My wealth is gone and will never return to me. A gift such as this is called a 'ruined gift' (*dānabhagna*); it is not a gift that brings about fame. What is the nature of such a gift? It is like a small amount of rice in a pot that is covered with a lid; it is smothered by the fire within the vessel. In the end, that small amount of rice in the pot turns to ashes, leaving nothing behind. Such is a gift that is ruined; it simply vanishes."
(Read *hilanga ta ya*?

by means of the *saraṅən sakukunan*. In brief: the gift disappears when it is marred by the anger of the intellect; the reason for this is that one must not be angry at the vessel [of the recipient] if one wishes to bestow the gift of merit.
A lake is indeed superior to a hundred wells; a sacrifice is indeed superior to a hundred lakes;
and a son is indeed superior to a hundred sacrifices.
Indeed, truth is far superior to even a hundred sons.

[Regarding] Kaliṅga: there is a man who digs a well with a spade; he obtains the fruit of digging a single pond. The man who digs a pond obtains greater fruit than the one who digs a well. There is a man who digs a pond with a spade; he obtains the fruit of that compared to a man who performs a sacrifice (*yajña*). Performing a sacrifice yields exceedingly great fruit. Furthermore, the man who performs a sacrifice with a spade obtains the fruit of that compared to a man who has only one child; if the child is distinguished, the fruit for that man who has a child is even greater. Again, the man who possesses many children obtains the fruit of truthfulness (*satya*). In brief, the fruit of the man of truth is greater; that is why he is called a *sādhu*. One must not be untruthful in one's vows (*vrata*) and in one's speech. Such is his conduct.
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood; for truth alone constitutes dharma in the three worlds—therefore, one should not violate the truth.
[Regarding] Kaliṅga: there is no dharma more profound than truth. Therefore, one must not forget the truth regarding that person.
The sin against an animal is tenfold; against a human, it is a hundredfold;
against a lord, it is ten thousandfold; and against a sage or a deity, it is infinite. 8.

[Śloka 08j] Regarding the Kaliṅga: a person who behaves like an animal has ten years as the limit for its lifespan; a person who behaves like a human has twenty years as the limit for its lifespan; one who behaves like a lord has one hundred years as the limit for its lifespan; one who behaves like a wise man (*paṇḍita*), and likewise one who behaves like a god, there is no limit to its lifespan. Thus says the venerable scripture.
Youth and beauty are impermanent; the accumulation of wealth is impermanent; union with loved ones is impermanent; therefore, one should practice the Dharma. 9.

[Verse 9j] Regarding the Kaliṅga people: their youth and physical form do not correspond to their birth; their abundance and accumulation of wealth do not correspond to that [birth]; furthermore, the person who eats and drinks along with his wife does not correspond to that [birth]. Therefore, one’s conduct must indeed be *dharma*, so as not to be stained by the state of being born again. One is able to reach the end of all that is maintained in the teaching of *dharma* from a wise teacher, provided one does not commit evil. Such is the sequence of becoming born again.
Wealth remains behind at home, while friends and kinsmen stay at the cemetery;
only one's good and evil deeds follow like a shadow.

[Kaliṅanya: This silver coin, adorned with jewels and the like, is entirely made of metal; it is struck by the hammer of the smith. When it is worn in the house, it is cherished by children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. If the descendants and lineage live wrongly, it becomes their ruin; it becomes a curse that brings about their destruction. However, when the children belong to a noble class, it is cherished in the cemetery. A "cemetery" (*śmaśāna*) means a place where those who have gone astray lie. The various ways in which it is struck by the hammer of the smith—whether through evil or good conduct—are struck until the vital breath (*prāṇa*) vanishes. If that conduct is wicked, it results in hell; if that conduct is virtuous, it results in heaven. The vital breath goes forth and is reborn; that is its destination. When the vital breath is born again, having been struck by evil or goodness, that is what is called "retribution" (*patayan*). This is the reason why.
(Emendation: *patañyan*)?

It is for those who know the *kaliṅga* that there exists what is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*). This is the statement of the venerable teacher (*ācārya*). Now, as for that which is derived from [the root] *in-tas*:
*(Note: The text provided contains several emendations; the translation reflects these corrections.)*
Hell: this is the sixth birth.

One who has no offspring, one lacking desire for pleasure, a eunuch, one who is weak, one whose penis is cut off, one who is impotent, one with fleshy growths, one with bilious disorders, one with a deformed tongue, one with extra fingers, one who urinates excessively, one with parted lips, and one who is deaf—[these are the defects]. 11.
Invited, intoxicated, and afflicted with leprosy; one whose belly is diseased, one who has departed;
the lame, the humpbacked, the blind, the one-eyed, the short-statured, the phlegmatic, and the one with a diseased eye. 12.

*Kaliṅga* means one who has no offspring; *anapatya* means one who does not procreate; *akāmaraśa* means one who is impotent; *klība* means one who is eunuch-like; *vadhri* means one who is castrated.

The meaning of *strī* is "not a woman. *Kilu* means a person with protruding teeth; *māṃsī* means a person with a goiter; *pittī* means a person who eats [excessively], having a distended belly; *kujiḥva* means a person who is mute; *aṅgu* means one who stammers; *mūtrī* means one who urinates [inappropriately]; *bhinnoṣṭha* means one whose lips are parted; *vadhira* means deaf; *nimatta* means blind; *unmatta* means insane; *kuṣṭha* means one afflicted by leprosy; *rogakukṣi* means one suffering from chronic abdominal diseases; *vigantika* means war; *khañja* means lame; *kubja* means hunchbacked; *andha* means blind; *ekadṛk* means one-eyed.
(One who has a single prominent eye, or, according to OJED, one with a single protruding eye)

*Hrasva* means the anus; *bāhu* means the testicles; *śleṣman* means phlegm; its root is the navel; *kunetra* means any disease of the eyes that serves as its ornament; its essence is darkness. All these are the signs from the pit; their end is liberation from hell in the world of Yama. They are placed within the middle state (*madhyapada*), which is the reason why the intellect must abandon all fear of hell, for this is the destination of those born into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

The cause of transmigration (saṃsāra) is the venerable Lord Yamarāja; furthermore, he imprisons those people who are led astray by an unwholesome intellect. They transmigrate through various states of existence, creating [their own karma]. However, there is no transmigration for the wise man (*paṇḍita*), for his [intellect] is purified. Even if one is a great deity, if their intellect errs, they are negligent like a deer caught in a snare; such is their condition.
A living being is a hell for the gods; a beast is a hell for living beings;
a wild animal is a hell for beasts; and a bird is a hell for wild animals.
For birds, the snake is a hell; for snakes, the fanged beast is a hell;
for those with fangs, the venom is a hell; and for those with venom, the slaying of men is a hell.

[Śloka 13–14j] Regarding the Kaliṅga: that which is observed by the intellect is what is called *janma-kelī* (the birth-cycle). It is like a fish observing water; its nature (*prakṛti*) is one of doubt, and it is difficult for it to reach the divine realm (*deva*). Even if it should return to the human state, this is very rare. One who is manifest (*vyakti*) and difficult to purify toward the divine becomes a human. A human whose intellect is defiled becomes a beast (*paśu*). A beast whose intellect is defiled becomes a lesser beast (*alpapaśu*). Now, there is the jackal, which is a lesser beast. The lesser beast is fortunate among those who are considered common; it descends further to become a deer. That deer is defiled in its intellect; it descends further to become a bird and a fish, for they are both born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*). Those birds and fish are defiled in their intellect among those considered common; they descend further to become snakes. Snakes are fortunate in that they kill with their fangs, for they are extremely cruel. They descend further to all those that are venomous and most cruel, eating even those considered common. This is the descent to poison (*viṣa*). Poison kills the life-force of beings; its nature is the *kālakūṭa* poison, the essence of destruction. It is said to be something that does not descend, known as the "essence of the abyss" (*hitip niṅ kavah*). Its sole function is to protect the roots of the forest. Its domain exists within the crevices of the earth. However, according to the Brāhmaṇas, Śaivas, Sogatas (Buddhists), and many who practice scholarship, it is not appropriate for them to consume it. Even if they were to eat it, or even if they were to vomit it out for a great reason, it is still not appropriate to do so, because it destroys the "essence of the abyss. Thus says the Holy Scripture: "It is not to be consumed."
Non-violence, celibacy, purity, moderation in food, and non-stealing—these five are the restraints (yamas) proclaimed by Rudra. 15.

[Kaliṅanya: "Behold the conduct of the Brāhmaṇas! O serpent-like Śaivas and Sogatas, they debate whether [the self] is eternal or non-eternal; their so-called 'non-violence' (*ahiṃsā*) means simply not to kill. They merely practice asceticism and vows. Regarding their practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), there are three kinds as follows: the white celibate (*śukla-brahmacārī*), the variegated celibate (*śavala-brahmacārī*), and the black celibate (*kṛṣṇa-brahmacārī*). This one is the black celibate, who is permitted to have sexual intercourse with his wife and his children, because the intellect of the wife and child is not yet mature; for both the mother and the woman [are not yet fully developed], provided that they do not conceive."

(Concerning) the sound: as long as she was small, there was no birth of a female child; her heart was distressed because of that crying and the sound, due to the smallness of her daughter. She spoke her true feelings. Such is the sequence of the householder;
do not be distressed.
Do not abandon that [person] (emendation: do not abandon that person who is wise?).
Furthermore, one should not act in such a manner toward a person of integrity, even if that person has committed an offense.

(Emendation: *sira hiyaha?*) O wise one, may your head be auspicious! May you be vigilant if he should be angry; how could it not be appropriate for you to go to him? Such is the sequence. Purity (*śuddhi*).

Its meaning is: constantly purifying the impure body; serving the sun; performing worship; reciting mantras; and offering oblations. *Āhāralāghava* (lightness of food) means moderation in eating; one should not eat anything that is considered forbidden (*dinalih*) in the world. However, if one eats such forbidden things, it must be done by one who observes pure vows (*śuddhabrata*), and not by those who are Brahmins, Śaivas, or Buddhists. *Janmatuccha* (worthless birth) refers to a transgression (*pātaka*). It does not suffice to merely reach the depths of one’s own spiritual pit. *Astainya* (freedom from greed) means not being envious of the wealth of others, not coveting the property of others, and not harboring evil intentions toward others in future lives. Even if one possesses great inner strength (*sattva*), one must remain vigilant. However, if one is found to be corrupt by others, one must not feel fear.
(Read *trāsa ri* with manuscript D) within the heart;

it is merely a matter of speaking. That indeed is what is called the *yamavrata*. Thus spoke the venerable Ācārya: "The Lord Rudra has revealed this secret teaching (*śāstra*). Great indeed is the fruit for one who practices the *Śaivasiddhānta* vow."
He who is virtuous in Dharma, who has conquered pride and anger, who is disciplined by knowledge, who does not harm others,
who is content with his own wife, and who avoids the wives of others—
For him, there is no fear whatsoever in the world.

[Śloka 16j] Kaliṅanya: Fulfill your ascetic practice (*tapa*). You are a serpent of the Śaiva Siddhānta; uphold the Dharma. Practice the noble conduct (*śīla*). Do not harbor pride (*māna*); conquer that pride. Do not be contentious with others—that is what is called anger (*roṣa*). Do not be arrogant in your mastery of all the sciences (*sarvaśāstra*); you have no need for boasting.
(Read *matakvan*—see OJED *butuh*)

The authority of all scriptures consists of verses and other statements. One must not harbor in one's mind what has been heard during the day; that which is spoken in sweet words is because of contentment with one’s own wife. "One’s own wife" (*svadāra*) means she who is dear to one’s heart; this is the reason for being devoted to one’s own four wives. "Avoiding another’s wife" (*paradāravarjī*) means not coveting the women of others; such is its purpose. He has no fear in this world. However, if he is reviled by others, his fault is not appropriate [to him]. To keep it secret so as not to cause mental distress is *uttama* (best). To speak of the matter within one’s heart is *madhyama* (middling). To speak of the matter so that it spreads through sound is *kaniṣṭha* (lowest). When one conceals the matter entirely, that is the *kaniṣṭha* of the *kaniṣṭha*. Thus says the Holy Scripture.
Having reflected for a long time upon the greater and contrary decline of others and his own,
the wise man disregards the process of decay.
One should provide a remedy for that; otherwise, it will not be so.

[Kaliṅanya: A "kṛtī" is the name for a wise person (*paṇḍita*). Let him not grieve over the illness that has befallen him. Even if it is incurable according to the physicians, he should not be distressed by it. He should merely endure his illness with fortitude, subduing the pain and its dissolution. Choosing the path of life, he makes it a ladder to the hereafter, a support for departing to the world of Śiva. Indeed, one must attain it through the application of ethical conduct (*śīlayukti*), as well as the ascetic practices and vows (*tapabrata*) of the monk; this is the application of destruction (*kṣayayukti*), which is equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The meaning of *kṣayayukti-upekṣā* is as follows: there may be a wicked person who intends to cause harm to him; he employs his ministers to deal with this. He does not experience the affliction of that calamity; rather, it becomes his own misfortune. This is what is called a "counter-measure" (*pratikāra*): the reversal of the illness or calamity. It is the divine punishment (*devadaṇḍa*) for those who cause harm, since they themselves become the instruments of his treasury and vehicle. This is solely due to the power of his asceticism and vows (*tapabrata*). Thus, the wicked person who committed the evil act suffers the pain from him. Such is the method of the wise man (*saṅ paṇḍita*).
The protector of the earth, accompanied by his army, treasury, mounts, and a multitude of ministers,
was defeated in battle by King Arjuna; though he was not slain,
his pride was shattered, his fortitude, heroism, and prowess vanished, and he lived on, censuring his subjects.
In birth after birth, he becomes impotent; having gone to death, he is not exempt from it. 18.
Corrupt Kaliṅga;
he is that king;
you (are he).

O King! The land is being ravaged; what is the state of your army, treasury, and vehicles? Why does the minister remain silent before the Lord? He is trembling in the midst of battle. His face is pale and his voice falters; at last he dies of fear. He is paralyzed by the enemy’s attack upon his person. The king’s pride has vanished. What will become of him if he flees? He is clearly despised by the entire kingdom. Yet, his steadfastness, heroism, and eloquence— (Note: The provided text appears to be Old Javanese prose with some phonetic or orthographic variations. The translation aims to convey the narrative flow of a king confronting a crisis, the failure of his ministers, and the loss of royal dignity.)
(em. *kaśūranira?* / *kaśaktinira?*) | "Suruda" means that the divine Mṛtyu is not barren regarding his life; it is there that his birth is made (*maṅdadi*).
O powerful one! It is said that the birth of a *kṣatriya* is to be fierce in battle;
it is not his conduct [to be otherwise].
Likewise, a monk who is fierce in his ascetic observances (*tapabrata*) is like the sin of a king who gives way to his enemy. This indeed is the royal governance of the wise; thus is its sequence.
Having the form of a lion in the midst of battle, speaking sweetly among women, yet a knower of reality among sages— he, being thus disciplined, entered the city.

[Verse 19j] Regarding the Kaliṅga: That man is worthy of being given [as a gift] when he is in the midst of battle, like the form of a lion; there is no fear of enemies. However, when among an assembly of women, his speech is sweet. But when among an assembly of wise men (*paṇḍita*), he understands and explains the truth. There is indeed such a person who is fit to be the protector of the city: a *kṣatriya*, a minister; such is the teaching.

One who knows the treatises, is of noble birth, is devoted to the reality of the Dharma, is impartial, and possesses intelligence is designated as the Superintendent of Dharma (dharmādhyakṣa). || 20 ||
[Sloka 20j] Regarding Kaliṅga: that which is suitable for it is a supervisor (adhyakṣa).

Now, regarding the qualities required: one who is "learned in the scriptures" (*śāstrajña*) is one who possesses no superior over him among all the scriptures and traditions (*śāstrāgama*). "Endowed with noble lineage" (*kulasampanna*) means that his ancestry is great. "Devoted to the truth of Dharma" (*tattvadharmaparāyaṇa*) means he is fond of the essence of the teachings of the Holy Dharma. His intellect is free from partiality toward others; even if there are many children, grandchildren, or kinsmen, or if they are of wicked mind, he does not show favoritism. This is what is meant by being impartial. Such a person is appointed as the Overseer of Dharma (*dharmādhyakṣa*). It is fitting for one who knows to be the overseer; this is the governance of the wise. Thus speaks the learned man who is master of the scriptures.
Wine, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī—these are the causes of intoxication;
he whose mind is not intoxicated by them is considered a true man.

[Śloka 21j] Regarding the Kaliṅga: that which is called *amuhara* (the mouth) is the person (*puruṣa*). It has three types: namely, *surā* means the skin; *sarasvatī* is the name of the divine Word (*saṅ hyaṅ aji*); and *lakṣmī* is the name of prosperity. Gold and silver—these are the causes for the purification of the mind. However, if there is a person who is not purified by the skin, by the divine Word, or by the prosperity of gold and silver, he is not what is called a *puruṣa*. If there is a person such as this, he is clearly sought after by the world. Thus says the divine Word.
Indeed, speech that may be used for jest, or for the protection of life and property, or regarding women at the time of marriage—these five kinds of untruth do not constitute a sin. 22.

[Kaliṅanya] | There are five things that do not bring about the sin of theft: namely, taking what has been abandoned; speaking the words of the Śiva-scriptures repeatedly; protecting one’s life; protecting one’s property; protecting one’s children and grandchildren; and furthermore, taking from a place where people congregate. One who steals in such a manner is capable of stealing.
The course of rivers, of creepers, and of women is crooked;
if a woman were truly virtuous, a white lotus would grow upon a stone.

[Sloka 23j] Kaliṅanya: There are three things that do not exist in this world; their forms are as follows: a river, a mountain peak, and the birth of a woman—these are the three. Their nature is deceptive; even if a woman possesses the wisdom of a Buddha, she becomes a mountain peak that grows upon a rock. In brief: there is no such thing as a mountain peak that can grow upon a rock. Thus says the Holy Scripture: [Sloka 24s-ab] Those endowed with beauty and youth, born of noble lineages...
Those devoid of knowledge do not shine, like *kiṃśuka* flowers lacking fragrance.
[Sloka 24j] There was a certain person who was exceedingly devoted to beautiful form and was in the prime of youth;
yet he was unskilled in all the sciences (*sarvaśāstra*) and possessed no knowledge whatsoever, even regarding the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*).

(Emendation: *sarvaśāstra*? Who is that person? He is not insignificant in the midst of the assembly. What is his nature? Like a *palāśa* flower, which has fragrance within its core but emits no scent when it is plucked; such is his character.
Honey produced from poisonous flowers is wholesome;
indeed, milk is produced from the blood and flesh of a buffalo.
Even a fragrant lotus has mud as its source.
With respect to the specific qualities of a person, caste is not at all a valid means of knowledge.

[Sloka 25j] Regarding the *kaliṅga*: honey is extremely beneficial in its medicinal taste (*pathyarasa*). It arises from the nectar of the *lataṅ* and *apituvī* flowers; nevertheless, it is pure. So too is the human being: he arises from the blood and flesh of the buffalo; nevertheless, he is exceedingly pure and possesses an excellent medicinal quality. So too is the *tuñjuṅ* (a type of jasmine): it arises from a foul-smelling stalk; nevertheless, it is exceedingly pure and possesses an excellent fragrance. Such is the person of distinguished qualities; there is no fixed measure for one's birth (*jāti*). Thus says the Holy Scripture (*śāstra*).
Nectar should be taken even from poison, and gold even from filth;
supreme knowledge is received even from a low person, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family. 26.

[Regarding] Kaliṅga: nectar (*amṛta*) is fit to be extracted from poison; gold is fit to be extracted from dross, dung, and excrement; the noble teaching of the *śāstra* and *āgama* is fit to be extracted even from a person of low birth; and a jewel among women (*strīratna*), even if she be of humble origin, is fit to be extracted. Thus it is with the teaching.
The Vaiśya born of a Vaiśya should be made a farmer, a cowherd whose vow is to support himself by grain;
engaged in trade, possessing a house, he is then a guardian of the fields.

[Regarding] the Kaliṅga: the duty of the Vaiśya is to cultivate the fields, to protect the cattle, and to guard the threshing floor. He should have a large bull as his companion. His dwelling is in the house; that which is called *kṣetrapāla* is the protector of the fields. This is the ordinance for the Vaiśya. Thus says the venerable scripture.
The wives of merchants are makers of wares; these are the various classes of merchants.
Then there is the business of buying and selling; furthermore, the Śūdra may engage in the activity of trade.

[Kaliṅga]: The Śūdra’s duty is to serve; he is one who is base and lowly, devoted to the pursuit of material wealth, and whose occupation is trade and commerce. This is the teaching for the Śūdra, the mark of the venerable Lord. Furthermore, as for those of the *antyajāti* (outcaste) class: they are indeed those who have transgressed; they are born from other lineages within the kingdom. This is the mark of the venerable scripture.

The grinder of perfumes, the brewer of liquor, the dyer with indigo, the washerman, the potter, the slaughterer of living beings, the smelter of minerals, and the weaver—these are the eight *caṇḍālas*. 29.

[Sloka 29j] Regarding the Kaliṅgas: these are the eight outcastes (cāṇḍāla) in the world: the grinder of grain, the maker of mats, the brewer of liquor, the dyer with indigo, the potter, the butcher, the metal-smelter, and the washerman. These are the eight outcastes according to the definition of the scriptures.
Those who have strayed from their own duties and subsist on the work of others,
and who despise the status of the twice-born— one should treat them as if they were Śūdras.

[Sloka 30j] Regarding the Kaliṅga: if there is a person who abandons his own lineage and instead serves every single one of the elders of other lineages, eating their leftovers and performing all the tasks for other people—that is what he makes his livelihood from. If it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Ṛṣi, a Śaiva, or a Sogata (Buddhist), it is the same; his lineage is lost through his association with those other lineages. That is not right. He has acted by taking up the work of the eight *cāṇḍālas*, thereby becoming their equal, because his action was wrong. In short, let no one born of pure lineage speak wrongly, act wrongly, or behave wrongly. Furthermore, regarding a Kṣatriya or a Minister (*mantrin*), even if they have fallen from their proper rank step by step, they are still superior in birth within the kingdom. Even if they have lost their rank and become fit to be gathered among the *cāṇḍālas*, they remain superior to those of impure lineage. Such is the case; this is a fault of the Lord. It is like a person of noble birth who is common, yet is given a turban, a head-ornament, a high seat, a canopy, and a parasol; the one who gave them these did not do so out of personal whim, but because that which was done was priceless.

He shall attain it. There is no need for ritual offerings (*karika*) or *bendu* for one who is graced by Him. Thus does the Lord, the Supreme Cause, bestow grace upon the lineage. The virtues and prowess of such a birth are not in vain; there is no conflict with the grace of the Holy One (*saṅ hyaṅ anugraha*) in such a birth. Even if one should become an animal—a being of the lowest quality—the Lord is not angry with such a person. This is what is expressed in the words of the Master.
Even a man who is destitute should not perform a blameworthy deed;
for even a tiger with severed paws would never eat grass.

[Kaliṅanya: That virtuous person is one of noble birth; even though he is poor, who here would not respect him? He is indeed praiseworthy in his conduct and praiseworthy in his way of life. Such is that person of noble birth, even as he falls here like a *śārdūla*. *Śārdūla* means a tiger: its claws are sharp, and it eats its food with its teeth, yet its behavior is not like that; for it is born with a keen sense of smell. Thus says the teaching.

One who sets fire to a dwelling, one who administers poison, one who practices the Atharva-veda for malevolent purposes, one who strikes with a weapon, one who violates another's wife, and a slanderer— these six, O King, are indeed assassins.

[Sloka 32j] Regarding *kaliṅgnya*: "An incendiary" (*agnida*) refers to a person who sets fire to forests or cities, or one who sets fire to houses for no reason whatsoever—whether it be the house of a deity, the house of a noble (*saṅ hyaṅ*), or the house of a wise scholar (*paṇḍita*)—such a person is an incendiary. "One who destroys the scriptures" (*śāstraghna*) refers to a person who subverts [the teachings]. "One who transgresses against his wife" (*dārātikrama*) refers to a person who is lustful and arrogant. "A slanderer of the king" (*rāja-piśuna*) refers to a person who betrays secrets; that is, one who slanders the sovereign or the minister by speaking words that cause harm to the state, all of which are born of envy and lead to evil deeds. Such a person’s speech is never true; he is merely a slanderer (*piśuna*). "Poisonous" (*viṣada*) means one who administers poison. "Sorcerer" (*atharva*) means one who performs sorcery, curses, casts spells, or employs various forms of black magic (*halahala*). All such practices are considered criminal acts; these are what are called the six types of assassins (*ṣaḍātatāyī*). These six kinds of actions are not merely human failings; they are sufficient to lead one to hell. Lord Yama seizes their life-force, and by the servants of the Holy One, their lives are taken away. This is their rebirth: if they speak, they are seized in the pit; they are trampled upon by the earth as if being crushed. Their death is abrupt and their bodies are mangled. Such is the condition of those who act in this way.
The leech is the moving form of evil, and the worm is that of excrement;
the world does not wish to display the forms of those things that lack stable form. 33.

*Kaliṅganya* (its meaning): *jalaukā* means leeches; *jaṅgamapāpa* (mobile evils) means all those that crawl about without feeling, which do not even know how to move. Such as, for example, worms in excrement—worms in filth, in the feces of elephants, in the dung of horses, and so forth. Furthermore, like the insects in excrement, they are entirely composed of insects; they have no form of bone, yet they are all slippery, crawling about without strength, moving only by their own nature. Such as, for example, *vaḍit*, *kuricak*, *hiri-hirispoh*, *caciṅ*, *varya-varya*, and so on—all these various small creatures in the world. This is what arises from one who commits the six types of heinous crimes (*ṣaḍātatāyin*) in this world. Even a slight deed of theirs becomes a sin that is difficult to escape. Thus says the Holy Scripture.
A face shaped like a lotus petal, speech as cool as sandalwood,
and a heart joined with a knife— these are the characteristics of a rogue.

[Regarding] the Kaliṅga woman: she has a body that is beautiful; her face is like a makara; her voice is sweet, like the sound of a makara crossing the water; her breath is fragrant, like the scent of sandalwood smeared upon the body. She is pleasant at all times, exceedingly charming to a man who is infatuated with her. Yet, what is within her heart is like a *kartra*—*kartra* meaning a sword. It is like the blade of one who wields a sword; it is sharp. Her envy is intense, causing distress and destroying the neck of even a virtuous and beloved man. Her nature is to cause harm; her speech is like honey mixed with poison. The sweetness of a long-standing [relationship] is the very cause of its downfall. This is the characteristic of the wicked.
The meaning of "the characteristics of a rogue" (*dhūrtalakṣaṇa*) is as follows:
he is the manifest fire of the *kālakūṭa* poison; he is the very form within the depths of the pit. In short, he does not harm even those of the most excellent birth.
Thus says the venerable *Śāstrāgama*.

Whatever good or evil a person performs as a child, a youth, or an old man, he experiences the results in each respective state of existence, birth after birth.

[Kaliṅanya: Regarding that which is done by a person while young: the fruit thereof will be experienced as pleasant in another birth when one is old. However, if one does what is evil, that evil will be experienced at the time of old age. Furthermore, if one grows up in the middle stage [of life], whatever good a person does, the fruit thereof will be experienced as good when one has grown old; but if one does what is evil, that evil will be experienced at the time of old age in another birth. Moreover, if one acts while mature, the fruit thereof will be experienced as good at the time of maturity in another birth; but if one commits evil, that evil will be experienced at the time of maturity in another birth. Thus it is said: there is no doing of good or evil that is not experienced, until its fruit is met in one’s final birth. For this reason, one should indeed cultivate a noble intellect from youth, so that upon reaching old age, one may experience fortune consistent with what was done in youth. Upon reaching maturity, it shall be the same. Such is the teaching of the Holy Scripture.

What use have deer who delight in grass and *kuśa* grass for gold? What use have monkeys who delight in fruit-bearing trees for jewels? What use have pigs who delight in what is foul-smelling for fragrant scents?
And yet, that specific excellence does not become dear to men.

[Śloka 36j] Regarding the Kaliṅga: the deer, the elephant, and the monkey—these do not find pleasure in their own skins when they serve as vehicles, seats, or ornaments. However, if those same skins are used for their own benefit—when they are in the forest, where their many hides are beautiful, soft, and supple—that becomes a source of joy to them. It is the same with the bee: it finds no pleasure in all manner of fragrant scents; rather, that which brings it pleasure is dwelling among the foul-smelling beeswax, for that is what delights its mind. In the same way, a person who acts contrary to his own nature does not find happiness. But this is not so for everyone; each person has a specific preference for their own skin (nature), which is what is cherished in their heart. This is the cause of the diversity of human birth: there are those who are noble, those who are charming, those who are base, those who are divine, those who are deluded, those who possess virtue, those who are deformed, those who are handsome, those who practice evil, those who practice good, those who are human, those who are *sattva* (beings), trees, creepers, and grasses. Within these distinctions, one can discern heaven and hell. What is their form? When there is a person who possesses absolute mastery over his own domain, that is called "heaven," and he is favored by the venerable Indra. When there is one who possesses compassion, he is a manifest *vidyādhara*. When there is a nobleman (*bhujaṅga*) or a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and is unerring in the truth of all scriptures and traditions, he is called the venerable Vṛhaspati. Furthermore, when there is a person who is deformed, deluded, wretched, or whose suffering is intense, that is called "hell. All animals are beyond description; from the grass, the tree, the creeper, down to the ant—all those that have breath are in hell. Therefore, one must perform virtuous deeds. By acting thus, one avoids the Great Roar (*mahārorava*) of hell. He who knows this knows the sublime Dharma. If the wisdom of Dharma is absent, it is said that one falls into the Great Niraya (Hell). *Nir* means "no," and *aya* means "going"; it signifies not proceeding toward the sublime Dharma. This is why one is tormented by the fire leading to the pit. This is the path leading to heaven. Thus spoke the venerable Dharma; such is the teaching of the scripture.
Bravery, health, and blameless pleasure; devotion to the gods, the acquisition of gold,
being dear to kings, and being dear to virtuous people.
[Śloka 37s-d] This, it is said, is the sign of those who have fallen from heaven.

[Śloka 37j] Regarding the Kaliṅga: there is that which is called *svargacyuta* (fallen from heaven). It refers to a person who, having already experienced happiness in heaven, has descended from the world of Indra (*indraloka*). However, it is not like that; rather, it is as follows: there is one of noble birth in a family, such as a lord (*prabhu*), or a disciple of one of noble birth, or one who is powerful, possessing great wealth, and whose intellect is fixed on Dharma. He knows the various births of human beings and is weary of worldly association. His horses are swift, and he is surrounded by male and female servants. He enjoys pleasures, indulges in sports, and takes wives from among people of high status—whether from the north, the south, the east, or the west—and he subdues the intellects of his enemies. He does not grant them the power to harm him; rather, he possesses everything. His speech is auspicious and respected, such that even Brāhmaṇas, Ṛṣis, Śaivas, Sogatas (Buddhists), and all those held to be learned praise him. His commands are never disregarded, nor are they ever contested; he punishes only when there is no fault. If there is a person whom he must punish, he punishes him only after the person’s guilt has been proven and recorded according to the authority of the scriptures (*āgamapramāṇa*). Thus, the nature of his governance is clearly seen: he eliminates wickedness through the agency of the overseer of Dharma (*dharmādhyakṣa*). When punishment is meted out, it is in accordance with the gravity of the offense, and the protector of the land punishes severely. Those who have offended him feel no fear, for their punishment is righteous Dharma intended for the correction of wicked persons. If there is a person such as this, even if he dies, he pursues excellent Dharma even at the cost of his life. This makes for his supreme merit (*kottaman*), leading him to be reborn as a lord, whether as a preeminent ruler over the earth. Such is the nature of his deeds: heroism (*śūratva*) means possessing valor in battle, being without shame before one's enemies; health (*ārogya*) means being free from illness throughout one's life; popularity (*rati*) means being cherished by the people; devotion to the gods (*deveṣu bhakti*) means having great devotion toward the Divine; acquisition of gold (*kanakalābha*) means extreme wealth in gold; and being beloved by the king (*rājapriyatva*) means being an object of the lord’s affection. These are the signs of a person who practices meritorious giving (*puṇyadāna*), who is virtuous and righteous among his peers. Such a person is said to have descended from heaven. Thus spoke the noble man.
Four kinds of people enjoy the earth adorned with golden flowers:
one who knows skillful means, a hero, one who is learned, and one who speaks kindly.

[Kaliṅanya: A person who is considered to possess a golden body in this world is as follows: one who knows how to employ means (*upāya*), and who knows the means used by an enemy; such a person is called *upāyajña*. One who is victorious in battle and has no adversary is called *śūra*. One who is discerning in the teachings of the scriptures (*śāstrāgama*) and has no doubt regarding all principles (*sarvatattva*) is called *kṛtavidya*. One who possesses many jewels of women, who is beloved by great men, and who, being skilled in the science of love (*anaṅgaśāstra*), is captivated by women, is called *priyaṃvada*. If there is such a person, he is a preeminent man who practices meritorious dharma (*puṇyadharma*). According to the scripture, such a person is chosen for his excellence in asceticism and vows (*tapabrata*).
The repeated utterances of many discourses and numerous statements, being refuted by that which is accessible through wisdom, should not be accepted by the discerning. 39.

[Kaliṅanya: Words that are unfit to be spoken by a wise person are unfit to be uttered by one who is served. *Vāda* means one who delights in contradicting his own sovereign. *Bahuvākya* means a sovereign who multiplies his words. *Vacana punah-punah* means a sovereign who does not heed his words. *Jñānagamya* means a sovereign who multiplies his desires; this leads to a lack of discernment (*viveka*). This is not the conduct of a sovereign; such is his fault. That which is called *vadva* is the impairment of his intellect, for the intellect of a ruler is easily agitated. It cannot be restrained by his ministers; it is difficult to serve. One cannot grasp all that he says. When a sovereign is thus, his governance becomes troubled. So says the Śāstra.
One should abandon a master who is excessively cruel; one should abandon a miser for being more cruel than that;
one should abandon an ignorant person for being more miserly than that; and one should abandon an ungrateful person for being more ignorant than that.

[Śloka 40j] Regarding Kaliṅga: A servant’s mind is devoted to his lord. If there is a king who does not act with discernment in his affairs, he becomes manifest as one whose mind is fixed on his enemies; consequently, that king becomes foolish and falls under the power of his enemies. If there is a king whose mind is thus fixed on his own subjects, he likewise becomes foolish and falls under the power of his enemies. To be "without distinction" (aviśeṣa) means to be confused. If there is a person of noble birth who is oppressed, and a person of low birth who is exalted—that is what is meant by being confused. If there is a king whose mind is thus confused regarding the birth of noble persons, then even so, that king becomes confused. To be "grateful" (kṛtaghna) is to be foolish. It means to be mad, lacking sense, lacking understanding, acting recklessly against people without cause, being arrogant toward people without cause, being envious of people without fault, and being destructive toward people without fault. All such actions of the ungrateful are considered wicked. If there is a king like this, he is extremely ill-fated in his dealings; he is not afraid to be cruel and harsh. He is like a monkey living in a forest tree: when its own minister strikes it, it becomes angry and does not yield, yet its heart is full of resentment. Thus spoke the Sage.
Neither sacrifice nor giving, nor the fire-oblation, nor celibacy, nor truthful speech;
neither the study of all the Vedas nor religious vows [can purify one].
That fruit which has been attained belongs to that which is not of this world.
[Śloka 41j] Kaliṅga said: "What is the reason for this? Look at the power of such a king! His valor does not fade; his gain is great, because he does not perform sacrifices nor does he bestow gifts."

O Paṇḍita, consider this: there are those who perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice, observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and speak only the truth; yet they do not understand the study of all the Vedas, they do not practice ascetic vows (*vrata*), and they lack respect for the Brāhmaṇas, the Śaiva sages, and the Buddhists. Nevertheless, they obtain results. This is because their vigor is not exhausted; the reason they obtain results is that their previous asceticism and vows have not been exhausted, and thus they receive gain without their effort being spent. However, there are some who, having already exhausted the fruits of their previous asceticism and vows, now find themselves on a path where they gain nothing. They do not perform sacrifices, nor do they bestow gifts upon the learned. When they die, they go to another world and are reborn into a low birth. There is no end to their births; they encounter ever-increasing suffering. They are tormented by various miseries, and throughout their entire conduct, they meet with evil and calamities. This is the state of those born now. Therefore, O Sovereign, one must never fail to exert effort and must always be firm in the noble Dharma. Upon death, one encounters once again the vigor of one's own nature. This is what makes a person what they are. It is like a person who has a field full of seeds: even if he does not gain any profit from it, the field will produce crops again, though not as abundant as before. This is the analogy: the body is the field, and the lineage is the seed. If the field is barren, nothing is produced. Yet, there are things that grow in it again; it is not so in reality. It is simply that the field is cultivated well, becoming fertile and productive. What is meant by "fertile"? It is that which causes the senses to flourish. What is meant by "productive"? It is the presence of greed, delusion, intoxication, pride, envy, and violence—these are called the six internal enemies (*ṣaḍvarga*). Greed means desiring the wealth of others to be acquired. Delusion means being deeply attached to one's possessions. Intoxication means being intoxicated by prosperity. Pride means having no sense of equality with one's peers, causing the body to become arrogant. Envy means being malicious toward one's fellow beings. Violence means committing acts of cruelty. These six enemies are the cause of sinful births. Even if one is born into a state of grace, the power of these six enemies remains. One cannot escape them; they are not easily overcome. One incurs sin, and even animals do not speak such things. How much more so for those who are wicked! Thus spoke the Holy Teacher.
A woman is weak and fickle, while a king is lacking in discernment;
therefore, a minister should indeed diligently abandon those who are unprotected from afar.

[Regarding] Kaliṅga: A woman whose husband is weak is fit to be abandoned. It is the same with a lord who is dull-witted; he is like a weak donkey that must be abandoned by its driver. Such is the nature of a king and his wife: if he is dull in establishing boundaries and does not protect her, she will surely fall away. Do not fail to exert effort in extracting the signs [of virtue]. Thus says the Holy Scripture.
The distiller of liquor, the worm-eater, the incendiary, the killer of living beings, and the potter—these five, along with the smelter of minerals, are proclaimed to be outcastes (cāṇḍālas). 43.

[Kaliṅanya: These are the ones known in the world as *cāṇḍālas*. There are five of them, namely: the *surāsut*, which means a person who drinks liquor; the *kṛmidāha*, which means a person who is impure; the *prāṇaghna*, which means a person who kills; the *kumbhakāraka*, which means a person who is deceitful; and the *dhātudagdhā*, which means a person who eats raw meat. These are the five. They are called *cāṇḍālas*; it is not fitting for people of noble birth to enter their dwellings. Such is the teaching of the *cāṇḍālas*. Thus spoke the venerable scripture.
Among birds, the crow is the outcaste; among wild animals, the donkey is the outcaste;
among men, the irascible man is the outcaste; but the wicked person is the outcaste of all.

[Śloka 44j] Regarding the bird, the *cāṇḍāla* is like a crow; regarding the deer, the *cāṇḍāla* is like a donkey; and regarding a human being, the *cāṇḍāla* is like a snake. Furthermore, the wicked person is worse than even a *cāṇḍāla*; he is surpassed by the wicked. That *cāṇḍāla* is superior, for he does not corrupt the common folk through his birth. Thus says the Holy Scripture.
He hears the voices of those who eat cows,
but I, O King, hear the words of the sages;
this has been witnessed by you as well with your own eyes.
Faults and virtues arise from association. 45.

[Śloka 45j] Kaliṅganyā: "If there is a person who does not associate with base people, his intellect will certainly become like that of a wicked and base person. Likewise, if one does not associate with virtuous people, his intellect will become like that of a virtuous person. There is an illustration for this: consider, for example, the two persons named Gāvākṣa and Girikā. The one named Gāvākṣa was eaten by an old monkey; he was despised. The one named Girikā was eaten by a wise man; he was honored. Once, there was a king who had many children. He was very fond of them and would carry them about on his shoulders. Once, while he was carrying one of his children on his shoulder, the child happened to fall onto the lap of a wise man. At that place where the child named Girikā was, the child cried out to its lord. It said: 'Alas! Alas! My skull is broken! Thus spoke the child. The lord laughed at its words, and the child became angry and went away. Finally, it went to the dwelling of the wise man. At the place where the child named Gāvākṣa was, it cried out. It said: 'Oh, what good fortune you have, O Lord! You have rescued my life! You have provided me with a dwelling! You have taken me as your son! You have protected me from the edge of the precipice, from falling into a pit, and from being swallowed by a wild beast, as well as from hunger and thirst. Because my life was difficult to save, I have come to you, O illustrious Great King. At that, the child spoke to him: "How strange is your heart, O Lord! To repeat the words of a child! Finally, the Lord questioned the wise man about the child that had been brought before him. The wise man said: "If it is through association that [character is formed], then, in brief, one should associate with virtuous people. Do not let him avoid associating with them, for they are those capable of cultivating virtues in him. Do not let him associate with wicked people, for he will fall into a pit. Thus spoke the Holy Teaching.
There is both fault and virtue; that which is entirely without fault is never born.
Just as for the lotus from the mud, there is no fault in its stalk because of its thorns.

[Kaliṅganyā: "That which is called a 'person' (*pudgala*) is not free from faults (*doṣa*). As long as a person is praised by the world for their virtues (*guṇa*), there exist those very flaws within that person, however great they may be—be it how much they know through study, how beautiful their form, or even if they are adorned with the marks of a noble birth. In short, there is nothing that does not decay and nothing that does not perish, just like a lotus flower; though it is said to be pure, what is it that truly remains? Thus speaks the world."
The lotus is full of thorns; the snowy Himalaya mountain is a sandalwood tree infested with serpents;
the sun is scorching; the moon has a body stained by a hare; the ocean has bitter water; Viṣṇu is a cowherd; the lord of the gods has a most fickle gait; and Śaṅkara has a blue throat.
All these are possessed of faults; how much more so, then, are the people on earth who are full of faults?

[Śloka 47j] Regarding instability: there is nothing that is not unstable. First, concerning sound: it is unstable; even the wind is unstable. A mountain is unstable because of its movement caused by snow; a sandalwood tree is unstable because its roots are shaken by fire; the divine moon is unstable because its fullness wanes; the ocean is unstable because its waters ebb; the divine sun is unstable because its heat waxes and wanes; Lord Viṣṇu is unstable because he rides upon a bull; the divine Indra is unstable because his elephant is restless; Lord Śaṅkara is unstable because of the poison Kālakūṭa in his throat. In short, there is nothing that is not called unstable. Even among the many gods, there are those who possess instability. How much more so for human beings? There is no entity whatsoever that is not unstable, whether it be small or large in its various distinctions. However, let all virtuous people understand this: a small fault is better than a great one. Thus says the Holy Scripture.
Like a king for five years, like a slave for ten years,
and like a friend at sixteen— this is the instruction for a son.

[Regarding] *kaliṅanya* (the time for it): "The bestowal of the boon upon the child occurs when he is five years old; it is like the Lord’s bestowing of a boon upon his own son. When that son has reached maturity, it is at twelve years of age; this is when the boon of my lord is bestowed as the best of boons. However, if the child is mature, it is at sixteen years of age; this is like a friend’s bestowing of a boon upon a friend. Such is the sequence of the bestowing of the boon upon the son, so says the Holy Scripture.
From indulgence arise many faults; from striking arise many virtues.
Therefore, with regard to sons and disciples, one should strike them and not indulge them.

[Śloka 49j] Regarding Kaliṅga: A son who is pampered is useless; he is not cherished and does not incur any fault. However, a son who is disciplined is useful even if he is struck day after day; he does not fail to acquire virtue. This is because both a son and a disciple must be struck in order for their virtues to increase. Therefore, do not grant them excessive indulgence. Thus says the teaching.

In giving a daughter in marriage, in clearing a debt, in the gift of the Dharma, and in acquiring wealth; likewise, in the face of enemies, knowledge, fire, or disease—one should not allow time to pass by idly. 50.

[Kaliṅanya: That which is not suitable for subduing is as follows: a daughter who is difficult to control; an ulcer that is difficult to heal; *dharma* that is difficult to practice; a month that is difficult to pass; an enemy that is difficult to overcome; knowledge that is difficult to master; fire that is difficult to extinguish; and disease that is difficult to cure. These are all things where there is no time for delay. Thus says the scripture.
Even another person who brings benefit is a kinsman, while a kinsman who causes harm is a stranger; a disease born of one's own body is harmful, whereas forest-grown medicine is beneficial.

[Sloka 51j] Regarding the Kaliṅga: A person who is truly wise is one whose body experiences happiness; this is what is meant by "kinsman" (*kadaṅ*). One who is not wise is one whose body does not experience happiness and constantly suffers; this is what is meant by "stranger. There may be a disease that afflicts the body, and one desires to treat it; this is what is called an "enemy" (*śatru*). However, the medicine provides happiness by curing the body and removing the affliction from the forest of suffering. Even though it is thus, it is cut, peeled, and sliced. Who has seen such a thing? It is like this, O Sugrīva: That monkey was killed by his own kinsmen, known as the *bālis*. But those two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, were truly strangers; nevertheless, they were protected by him in the midst of the forest and served as the medicine for the illness of Sugrīva. Such is the nature of kinsmen and relatives: if they do not wish to treat one’s body, they are called enemies. A person who is truly wise is one who seeks the well-being of the body; this is well-known as a "kinsman" (*kadaṅ sānak*). Thus spoke the venerable Sage.
The moon is the illuminator of the night, and the sun is the illuminator at dawn;
the Dharma is the illuminator of the three worlds, and a virtuous son is the illuminator of his lineage. 52.

[Śloka 52j] O Kaliṅga! When it is night, the venerable Moon is the witness; when it is day, the venerable Sun is the witness; when it concerns the three worlds, the venerable Dharma is the witness; and furthermore, when it concerns this family, the virtuous son is the witness. Thus says the scripture.
Born from the same sap and endowed with the same constellation,
they do not become uniform in their conduct, just like the jujube thorns.

[Regarding] Kaliṅanya: this child, though having emerged from the womb with great difficulty, was named Tuṅgala by his father and mother. All of his siblings were born at the same time and under the same lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) as he; nevertheless, his intellect did not match theirs at all. It is like a ripe *badara* fruit that has fallen and rotted; such is the intellect of the person who is called a "child. Thus says the Holy Scripture.
For one ensnared by the serpent-noose of a wife, for one possessed by affection for a son,
and for one consumed by the fire of craving— renunciation alone is the great medicine.

[Kaliṅanya: A woman is the poison; her tight embrace is the snake-noose that clings to the body, constricting the neck and crushing the heart of one who has a son. Yet, craving (tṛṣṇā) is what permeates the limbs; this is the venom. What is its antidote? Only renunciation (tyāga). Thus says the Holy Scripture (Āgama).
An old woman, a wealthy woman, and an ugly woman who is extremely industrious; a poor woman, and one endowed with beauty—these three should be served by the wise. 55.

[Kaliṅganyā] Regarding a person who speaks: if one has already consumed [wealth] after reaching old age, that person is a chatterer; if one is wealthy but speaks much, that person is a chatterer; furthermore, if one’s appearance is ugly yet possesses extreme wisdom, that person is a chatterer; however, if one is modest out of compassion and supported by the beauty of their form, that person is a chatterer. This is the third type of chatterer according to the wise, so says the scripture.
Even one destitute of wealth, if born of noble lineage; or even a twice-born man devoid of the Vedas;
or a king lacking servants—these are honored by the brahmins in this world.

[Kaliṅga: A person whose lineage is noble, yet who is Kasyapa—such a one is fit to be a king, for he possesses great majesty. What then of that Brāhmaṇa? Even though he is inferior regarding the Vedic scriptures, nevertheless, by virtue of his birth, he is fit to be a king. What then of that King? Even though he is inferior in speech, his army, treasury, and vehicles are vast; he is fit to be a king in this world. Furthermore, if he is a king, he is worshipped by the Brāhmaṇas, the Ṛṣis, the Śaivas, and the Sogatas (Buddhists); such is the mark of the venerable Lord.
Violence is the strength of the ignoble; forbearance is the strength of the virtuous;
the administration of punishment is the strength of kings; and service is indeed the strength of women.

[Verse 57j] Regarding the Kaliṅga woman: her power is wickedness; she considers her own birth to be superior. As for the man of noble character (*agə̄ṅ guṇa*), his power is the pacification of anger; "pacification of anger" means having love for all people, even toward those who are hostile. Even if his strength (*sattva*) is great, he exercises self-restraint. If there is an offense, such is the conduct of that king: his power is the application of punishment (*ḍaṇḍavidhi*). "Application of punishment" refers to that which is faultless according to the scriptures (*āgamaśāstra*) and so forth. Now, regarding the power of a woman: her power is service (*kaśuśrūṣā*). "Service" means being truthful to one's husband and acting in accordance with the wisdom of the master. Thus says the Holy Scripture.
Even for a serpent, poison resides in its fangs; for the fool, poison is considered to reside in his mind.
Paying homage to those who are harmful is poison; among women, a crooked disposition is poison.

[Sloka 58j] Kaliṅga: The snake in its hole is full of poison; such is the wicked fool—within his mind he is full of poison. Furthermore, the man who does not enjoy what is pleasant regards it as poison. And likewise the woman: she is attached to her husband and is full of poison. Thus says the Teacher.
Study is poison without practice; food is poison for one with indigestion;
social gathering is poison for the poor; a young woman is poison for the old. 59.

[Kaliṅanya: A person who has practiced the scriptures but whose desire does not cease—such a person makes the scripture itself into poison. It is like a person who eats food that is not digested in the stomach; though they have great desire for it, it becomes poison. Furthermore, as for a poor person, whatever is mentioned by them serves as their poison, because throughout their entire life they have always been deprived of wealth and have longed for riches. Thus says the teaching.
A maiden not yet in her season, a young woman, and one who has reached puberty; a beloved woman endowed with breasts—a woman struck down by the arrows of Love.

[Kaliṅanya: A woman who has menstruated is called *ravatravat* in Madanirīya; she is what is known as a *kanyā*. Furthermore, a woman who has abundant menstrual flow and is young is called a *yuvatī*. There is also a woman whose breasts have not yet developed; she is one who engages in sexual union, and she is called a *kāntā*. Next, a woman who has already been pierced by the arrow of the god of love (*smara*), who repeatedly dies and is born again through the power of passion, is called a *pramadā*. Thus says the Śāstra.
Knowledge multiplied a thousandfold is to be distrusted; even a king who has been propitiated is to be distrusted;
and the course of a wife, being crooked, is to be distrusted.
Even a horse is to be suspected because of its swift movement.

[Kaliṅanya: "This person who has mastered the meaning of the *śloka*—do not say that his mastery of the sacred science (*vidyā*) is exhausted. Even now, he is still being tested by the flavor of the scriptures; yet, even so, he remains capable of doubting the flavor of the sacred teaching again and again, for he cannot be overcome by those who wish to deceive him. Such is the king: however many are the troops gathered around him, along with his ministers, horses, elephants, chariots, and weapons—even so, he is worthy of being doubted by his enemies, for he cannot be overcome by enemies who come against him. Such is the woman who is taken as a wife: even though she may still be very young, and her husband may look upon her with affection—even so, she is worthy of being doubted in her intellect, for her foolishness cannot be overcome. Such is the horse: however many times it may be examined during its training—even so, it is worthy of being doubted in its manner of galloping, for it cannot be overcome. Thus spoke the venerable teacher.
A king finds no satisfaction in the accumulation of wealth;
the ocean finds no satisfaction with water;
and the wise find no satisfaction with well-spoken words.
There is no satiety for the eye from beholding that which is pleasing.

[Śloka 62j] Kaliṅga said: "O Lord, how great is the quantity of gold, silver, jewels, garments, and ornaments, as well as wealth, that he possesses! Nevertheless, his heart is not satisfied; he still desires even more of all kinds of goods. Yet he finds no contentment through them. It is just like the ocean: however much water it receives from the rivers flowing into it, it is never satisfied by those rivers pouring into the sea. Day after day, its waters do not cease to arrive. It is just so with the wise man (*paṇḍita*): however many sacred teachings (*śāstra-āgama*) he has studied, and however many virtuous or non-virtuous deeds (*karma śubhāśubha*) he has performed, nevertheless, despite all of these, he is not satisfied by them. He does not grow weary of performing meritorious deeds, nor does his thirst ever cease; all knowledge remains stored within him. It is just so with the faculty of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*): however much it sees according to its desire, nevertheless, it is not satisfied by seeing whatever is beautiful; it always desires to behold what is pleasing and beautiful again and again. Thus says the Holy Scripture (*Āgama*).
Even then, as if under the influence of the treatise, the satisfaction of the fool is like a creeping vine that spreads through mere outward appearance.
How could that lamp of the intellect's knowledge perceive a jar within a hollow? Where indeed has such a thing been seen?
Sloka 63c reads: "Why does he place the jar into the hollow?
(TL)

[Regarding] Kaliṅga: The knowledge of that wise man is absolute. He has internalized the teachings of the *śāstras* and *āgamas* within his heart, which possess great power. An illustration of this is as follows: it is like a firecracker placed inside a hollowed-out coconut shell. It is hidden within; it is not seen from the outside. Nevertheless, its presence is evident, for its smoke alone is visible, emerging and spreading outward. Such is the one who knows the *śāstras*. There is only a slight appearance of verses (*ślokas*) in the world, yet those who perceive them know what lies within. However, the deluded person is like a creeping vine: when it is scorched, it merely withers and shrivels up; it does not heal, but only dries away. In brief, the knowledge of the learned is like a firecracker; it must be examined by one who knows the Kaliṅga of supreme knowledge. Thus spoke the venerable Lord of Knowledge.
The twice-born, the one who bestows grace upon the deities,
the lord, and the one joined in yoga— these four are unfailing.

[Kaliṅanya: That which is not two is his word in the world: a Brahmin perfected in the four Vedas—he is not liberated; furthermore, one who has already received the grace of the gods—he is not liberated; furthermore, a king who has been a sovereign *cakravartin*—he is not liberated; a wise man (*paṇḍita*) who has completed the practice of special yoga and attained the knowledge of the partless (*niṣkalajñāna*)—he is not liberated. These are the four states that are not liberation. Thus says the Holy Lord.
They say that austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age, and knowledge in the Tretā;
they say that sacrifice is supreme in the Dvāpara age, and giving alone in the Kali age.

[Regarding the Kali Age: The conduct of the Kṛtayuga was as follows: a person who practiced asceticism (atapabrata) was considered superior; he was valued by everyone. However, in the Tretāyuga, knowledge (jñāna) was considered superior; "knowledge" here means yoga, which distinguished that person from others. Furthermore, in the Dvāparakāla, fire-sacrifices (homayajña) distinguished the person. What is the form of such sacrifice? It is the Aśvamedhayajña and others; these were considered superior. But as for the present Kaliyuga, silver, rice, and fish are considered superior by people. The reason for this is that he is a *sādhu* (virtuous one). There is suffering in the Kaliyuga, because it is tormented by wicked people (*durjana*). In brief: the wicked and the corrupt are made the bodies of the Destroyer (*saṅhāra*), because they cause the disappearance of virtuous people (*sādhujana*). Therefore, one who desires noble intelligence (*buddhi*) should not be slow to honor the *sādhu* and great scholar (*mahāpaṇḍita*). So that one does not incur the sins (*pātaka*) of birth in the Kaliyuga; for one does not consider the Destroyer to be sinful, since the person who is the Destroyer in the Kaliyuga is liberated from great sins. This applies even more so in the Kṛtayuga, the Tretāyuga, and the Dvāparayuga; in short, they become the objects of contempt. For the fault lies in insulting a scholar, in plotting against a scholar; the reason is that one incurs sin. Such is the excellence of the Yugas; this is called the state of the Wheel (*cakrabhāva*). Only the Kaliyuga is the time of happiness, because it serves as the nourishment for the intelligence of scholars and as the fuel for those who consume the kingdom. It is made the nourishment of all that is good; its essence is cultivated in the Kaliyuga. This is what makes all religious duties (*dharma*) its work. Thus spoke the Holy Scripture.
Primal Matter is like a cart, and the Person is like a bull;
joined with the Lord as the charioteer, the world revolves like a turning wheel.

[Regarding] Kaliṅganya: This person is the three ages; he goes back and forth with the Kaliyuga. The three ages together with the Yuga constitute the Pradhāna, who is the driver of the chariot (śakaṭa). The Puruṣa impels the intellect (buddhi) toward what is evil or good. The Puruṣa takes the form of a bull as his sign (nimitta); this was done by the Lord (Bhaṭāra) to mount the chariot. There is no end to the birth of evil or good. The Lord Īśvara is the charioteer of the body (paḍati); this was done by the Lord to drive it. He whips the oxen; they are the components of the Puruṣa. The four ages (caturyuga) are the axle-pin of the body, which is like a broken wheel. The meaning of that which is called "the old" (ṅūni) is the principle (tattva): the divine Sun and Moon are the two wheels of the broken wheel. The Moon is on the left, the Sun is on the right; their principle is that there are twelve Suns and twelve Moons, which is the cause for the completion of twelve months. The abbreviated axle-pin consists of four; the cause for the number twelve of the wheels is the completion of the months. The junction (buṅbuṅan) is the day and night; its principle is the divine Dharma wandering about. The principles of passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and the ten senses (daśendriya) are the deep interior of the axle-pin. Furthermore, all the filth is attached to that axle-pin. However, if a person in the Kṛta, Tretā, or Dvāpara ages is wicked and base, when they die and are born again, they will grow up in the Kaliyuga. But if a person in the Kaliyuga possesses virtuous intellect and character, when they die and are born again, they will grow up in the Kṛta, Tretā, or Dvāpara ages. If their intellectual character is abundant in the Kṛta, Tretā, or Dvāpara, their growth in those three ages will be abundant. However, if a person in the Kaliyuga has abundant intellect but becomes wicked, their growth in the Kali age will be abundant. As for the distinction of birth in the Kṛta, Tretā, or Dvāpara: if one reaches the time of the Kaliyuga, one does not descend to be born there again; one returns to the principle of Puruṣa, becomes a god, and dwells in the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Īśvara. When the time and month of the Kṛta, Tretā, or Dvāpara arrive, one descends again to be born as a human. Here is the distinction of people in the Kaliyuga: when the time and month of the Kṛta, Tretā, or Dvāpara are reached, one returns to the principle of Pradhāna, produces animal beings (tiryak sattva), and wanders through all things, from the immobile to the mobile. But if one is consumed and digested in the Kṛta, Tretā, or Dvāpara, those immobile and mobile beings become humans as the essence of what was consumed—just as when the fragrance of sandalwood is burned, its scent does not vanish. This is the cause for the decline of the ages due to doubt: the Kṛtayuga declines into the Tretā; the Tretā declines into the Dvāpara; the Dvāpara declines further into the Kali. The cause is that there is no mastery in performing knowledge (jñāna), no mastery in performing sacrifice (yajña), and no mastery in performing meritorious giving (puṇyadāna). Giving silver coins, rice, and oil—this is the manifestation of one who possesses doubt. Thus says the Holy Scripture (Āgama).
The gift of food is the lowest, and the gift of wealth is middling;
the gift of a daughter is supreme, while the gift of knowledge is infinite.

That which is yet to come is *kaniṣṭhadāna* (the lowest gift), namely when a person gives gold and jewels. *Madhyamadāna* (the middling gift) is when that person further gives his daughter. *Uttamadāna* (the supreme gift) is when that person upholds the sacred Dharma and the scriptural traditions (*śāstrāgama*), and instructs others in the right and wrong of conduct. *Anantadāna* (the infinite gift) is that whose fruit is never exhausted. Thus says the venerable *Āgamavidhi*.
One who does not approve of a donor who gives even a single syllable is reborn as a dog, and subsequently is born as a caṇḍāla. 68.

[Regarding] Kaliṅganya: The nature of human birth in the Kali Yuga is such that even if there is one who knows how to study the *śāstras* and *āgamas*, and has mastered the meaning of those *śāstras*, yet his letters are confused and his syllables are disordered; once he has been instructed, he may eventually reach the end [of his learning], but his reputation is such that he is not a scholar (*paṇḍita*) regarding that which I know of the *āgamas* and *śāstras*. "I know it thoroughly"—such is the brevity of birth in the Kali Yuga. If there is a person like this, he will have already exhausted the fruits of his karma (*karmaphala*). *Karmaphala* means the fruit of good and evil deeds; such a person will perish and finally return to the womb of a dog (*śvānayoni*). *Śvānayoni* means being born as a dog. When that dog perishes, he is born as a *cāṇḍāla*. What is the intellect of a *cāṇḍāla*? This is the progression of the birth of a *cāṇḍāla* arising in the Kali Yuga: there is a person who calls himself faultless, who repeatedly commits evil against virtuous people (*sādhujana*), who reviles the virtuous, who treats the wise with contempt, who insults ascetics (*viku*), who is licentious, who is promiscuous, who is treacherous, who is deceitful, who is malicious, who is cruel, who is arrogant, who is insolent, who is cunning, who is treacherous, who is deceptive, who is wicked, who speaks harsh and impulsive words, who envies those who are wealthy, who envies those who possess good fortune, who covets the property of others, who is full of malice toward those who are kind, even toward those who practice sacred vows (*tapabrata*), who is conceited regarding the logic of Dharma, who is deeply involved in the eight vices (*aṣṭaduṣṭa*) and the eight thefts (*aṣṭacora*), and the six types of assassins (*ṣaḍātatāyī*). He is deeply involved in insulting cows, insulting Brahmins, insulting *bhujaṅgas*, *ṛṣis*, Śaivas, and Buddhists, insulting his gurus, elders, and those of noble lineage. He steals the property of the gods (*devadravya*), takes disciples from his own guru, and takes disciples for himself. He steals the property of the Arabi Samanya Lanang and the Arabi Samanya Vadon. There are those who steal their mothers, and those who steal their children. They have no father, no ascetic, no maternal uncle, and no kinsman. Such is the conduct of the Kali-saṃhāra; there is neither above nor below. Furthermore, the kingdom is turbulent, the heavens are shaken, the stars are eclipsed, the years are deficient, the seasons are lost, and the villages are in chaos. The law of the people of the land, the boundaries, and the Dharma of prosperity all perish.
