The city is ruined; there is distress and poverty; there is intense hunger and the devouring of one another; and there is the loss of one's kin. One does not obey the Lord, nor does one honor one’s parents, siblings, elders, or teachers. Such is the nature of the intellect of people during the age of dissolution (*kali-saṃhāra*). However, those who have cultivated the sublime Dharma must not join in the confusion of the conduct of the wicked minds of the *kali-yuga*; they must remain as those who do not sink into the pit. Thus spoke the Holy Scripture.

The killer of a fetus, the murderer of a man, the thief of a maiden, one who performs the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice without the prescribed materials, and one who does not observe the annual ancestral rites (*sāṃvatsarika*)— these are proclaimed as the great sinners (*pātakin*).

[Kaliṅganya: "Bhrūṇahā" means one who kills an embryo in the womb. "Puruṣaghna" means one who kills a man. There are two kinds of such men: first, there is the man who is rich in virility and possesses excellence in his own region; he is called a *puruṣa*, and his name is "the wealthy one" (*dhanavān*). Furthermore, there is the man who is learned in many scriptures (*bahuśāstra*) and has no superior in the knowledge of the principles of the scriptures (*tattvāgama*); he is a *puruṣa*, and his name is "the possessor of scripture" (*śāstravān*). "A daughter-stealer" (*kanyācora*) means one who takes a maiden by force. "A chief sacrificer" (*agrayājaka*) means one who performs sacrifices for his own sake, seeking to satisfy his own desires, and does not observe the proper sequence of the ritual acts. "One who ignores the astrologer" (*ajñātasāṃvatsarika*) means one who errs regarding the months. If there is a person like this, he falls into a pit and becomes the innermost part of the realm of hell (*nirayapada*). Thus says the Holy Scripture.
The killing of a cow, the killing of a young woman, and the killing of children or the elderly,
as well as the burning down of houses— these are called secondary offenses (upapātaka).

[Sloka 70j] Regarding Kaliṅga: these are the transgressions of a person in the Kali Yuga. "Killing a cow" (govadha) means slaughtering an ox. "Killing a young woman" (yuvatīvadha) means killing a maiden. "Killing a child" (bālavadha) means killing a child who does not yet know how to live. "Killing an elder" (vṛddhavadha) means killing one who has already reached old age. "Burning a house" (āgāradāha) means setting fire to a dwelling. These are what are called secondary sins (upapātaka). If there is a person who acts in such a way, they shall fall into hell and become the fuel for the Great Hell (Mahāniraya). Thus says the Lord.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold,
obstructing a maiden’s marriage, and killing one’s teacher are declared to be the great sins (mahāpātaka).

[Kaliṅganya: Herein lies the description of the person in the Kali Yuga. "Killing a Brahmin" (brahmavadha) means slaying a Brāhmaṇa. "Drinking liquor" (surāpāna) means consuming that which is drunk by the Lord of the Śaiva Siddhānta [the serpent]. "Stealing gold" (suvarṇasteya) means plundering gold. "Violating a maiden" (kanyāvighna) means approaching a girl who has not yet reached the age of menstruation; she dies as a result of the sexual intercourse. Such a person is one who violates a maiden. "Killing a teacher" (guruvadha) means slaying a guru. These are what are called the "great sins" (mahāpātaka). If there is a person who acts in such a way, he shall fall into hell and become a resident of the Raurava realm. Thus says the Scripture.
He who consorts with his own daughter, he who consorts with his mother,
and he who takes up her emblems— this is called a transgression beyond the worst (atipātaka).

[Śloka 72j] Regarding *kaliṅganya*: one who violates his own daughter is called a *putrī-bhajan* (one who violates his daughter). One who violates his mother is called a *mātṛ-bhajan* (one who violates his mother). Regarding *liṅgagrahaṇa* (the seizing of the *liṅga*): it refers to a person who, being without a master (*anātha*), destroys a *liṅga*, an image (*arca*), a sacred grove (*kabuyutan*), or the house of a deity (*deva*). The destruction of a *liṅga*, an image, and so forth, by repeatedly damaging them—that is what is meant by *liṅgagrahaṇa*. Such is the nature of birth for people in the Kali Yuga; its cause is that it is not equal to the nature of people in the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages. Its nature is such that if there are people practicing their births in the Kali Yuga who possess extremely dull intellects, they take up the seizing of the *liṅga* (*liṅgagrahaṇa*). They fall into hell and become the innermost part of the Great Raurava realm (*mahāroravapada*). This is taught as the "extreme sin" (*atipātaka*). Thus says the venerable Lord (*liṅ saṅ hyaṅ aji*).
Of the blue lotus, the red lotus, the fish, and the night-lily—
though these are born from a single source, their fragrance is distinct for each.

[Kaliṅanya: *Utpala* means a blue lotus; *aravinda* means a red lotus; *kumuda* means a white water lily; *tuñjung* means a red lotus; *tuñjung sindūra* means a vermilion-colored lotus; *matsya* means a fish. These are all born from the same water, yet they differ in their appearance. Likewise, although they are of the same kind, they do not share the same fragrance. Such is the case for those born in the *kali-yuga*. One should not have the same understanding as the people of the *kali-yuga*. For he who acts according to his own intellect during the *kali-yuga* will suffer, even though his intellect may be like that of a person in the *kṛta-yuga*, *tretā*, or *dvāpara*. He must follow the excellent Dharma and strive to return to the state of a deity, for a human being was once a god. A deer is a yogi; it becomes a human being because of this. However, if one errs regarding this point, after having become human, one will perform actions (*akṛti*) that lead to the path of non-human beings—that is, birth. Birth is difficult to traverse, full of obstacles, and its entry is fraught with suffering if one does not abandon evil. This is evident when you observe the nature of animals and humans: their conduct is not far removed from each other. The Lord has distinguished them; animals lack specific knowledge (*jñāna-viśeṣa*), whereas humans possess it. Yet, there is no difference in how the Lord grants them life, for animals were also born as living beings who did not desire the aforementioned excellent Dharma. That is why there is nothing like the Holy Dharma to serve as the basis for returning to the state of a deity again. But if one lacks the fortune of the body, one falls back to the state of a human and performs actions again. One must choose carefully between the distinctions and the various births. What, then, is the fruit of the Holy Dharma when it is understood and practiced? There are two ways to attain it: namely, through *vīryavān* (the energetic) and *śāstravān* (the learned). How does the energetic one attain the state of a deity? His practice consists of the gift of Dharma (*dāna-dharma*). How does the learned one attain it? His fruit is possessed of the scriptures; his practice consists of austerity and vows (*tapas-brata*), and he dwells within the totality of reality (*sarvatattva*). The forms of origination, maintenance, and dissolution—these are the principles of the worlds (*bhuvanatattva*)—are known by the learned one in three ways. Thus spoke the Holy Scripture.
Wealth is an ornament in this world; pure wealth is the ornament of the face.
Wealth is the staircase to heaven; wealth is the warder-off of miserable rebirths.
[Regarding] Kaliṅganī: the month that serves as the substance for the wealthy; it is fashioned into an ornament.

Gold is long-lasting in this world; it is indeed a metal. Its fruit when used for improper purposes is that it burns the mouth [of the user]. However, if it serves as a means for the steps to heaven—namely, by giving it to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, or further, to a learned scholar (*paṇḍita*) whose mind is joyful and whose intellect is refined—then even though gold does not follow along with *dharma*, there is no gold that will fail to reach the one who has placed it there in the hereafter. One must choose carefully the gold that is to be offered as a gift; one must choose the path leading into the pit. If one errs, death is the consequence; this is why the wise man does not desire to swallow gold. He regards only the Holy Dharma as his gold coin, which he places within his heart; thus, even now, it reaches its destination in the presence of the Lord. Thus spoke the Holy Teacher.
Gold, when repeatedly smelted, regains its beautiful luster; sandalwood, when repeatedly rubbed, regains its lovely fragrance;
and the stalk of sugarcane, when repeatedly cut, regains its pieces once more.
Even at the end of existence, no transformation of their essential nature arises for the supreme ones.

[Regarding] *kaliṅanya*: Gold (*mās*) is that which is melted again and again; finally, its color becomes radiant, causing joy in those who behold its fruit. Such is sandalwood (*candana*): it is cut and split again and again until it reaches the very core of its wood; finally, there arises a doubt regarding the excellence of its fragrance, causing joy in those who smell its fruit. Now, as for the sugarcane (*təbu*): it is crushed into pieces from top to bottom until it reaches the stalk; finally, it is tasted when eaten, and the sweetness of its flavor is experienced. But where is the essence of that which is eaten? Regarding gold: one sees its beautiful form and color, the brilliance of its hue; but where is the end of the sight for the one who looks? Such is sandalwood: it is carried away and smelled by the fragrance; but where is the end of that smelling? And as for the sweetness of the sugarcane: the tongue tastes its sweetness; but where is the end of that taste? Regarding this: form (*rūpa*), fragrance (*gandha*), and taste (*rasa*)—these are the roots of birth and growth. These are *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and *vikṛti* (modification). That which is *vikṛti* returns to *prakṛti*, becoming a human being. That which is the Imperishable (*akṣara*) has no end to its arrival. That which is the Imperishable is eternal in the world. In brief: that which is not the self (*amoha*) in the world is the cause of the world’s arising and the cause of the world’s death. This is what must be understood in its essence and its function; this is what is called *dharma*. Thus says the Knower. That which grows, once destroyed, does not exist again; therefore, practice now so that you do not perish, and do not come [to ruin]. Thus says the Holy Scripture (*saṅ hyaṅ aji*).
After happiness comes suffering, and after suffering comes happiness;
thus everything in the world, both stationary and moving, revolves like a wheel.

[Kaliṅanya: This is the name of the kingdom. There is no one who does not experience pleasure and pain; these pleasures and pains do not cause them to be born again, nor do they choose their own lineage. Even in great abundance, there is no talk of pity, for the entire world has already been sacrificed—both the stationary and the moving. There is no longer any strife, for the cause of its existence is asceticism (*tapabrata*), yoga, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), meritorious giving (*puṇyadāna*), and Dharma. It is for the sake of overcoming suffering and attaining happiness, as a sign for those who know the Dharma, so that they do not desire to suffer while growing in equanimity (*samasameṅ*). They have offered up their own suffering in other births, for the sequence of the entire world is such that the high becomes low and the low becomes high; the forward-moving becomes backward-moving, and the backward-moving becomes forward-moving; the pure becomes impure and the impure becomes pure. This is the reason for those who know the Dharma: they do not desire to make the property of others impure. Such is their way of life, intended to refine the intellect of all who grow together, so that they do not cause pain to the hearts of others. Thus spoke the Holy Scripture (*saṅ hyaṅ aji*).
Both the guest and the critic are my two kinsmen;
the critic removes my sin, while the guest leads me to heaven.

[Kaliṅganya: Regarding the guest (*atithi*): it refers to a person who arrives unexpectedly (*kasyasih*), coming to one’s household by chance. One should not treat them with negligence due to their unfamiliarity. The result of such hospitality is that the wealth of the host leads him to heaven. This is what is called honoring a guest (*pūjātithi*). Regarding slander (*apavādī*): do not seek out faults in others; do not speak of evil, even if it be the truth of evil. To seek out faults in evil is not right; it is the very nature of a slanderer to seek out faults. By seeking out faults and speaking of evil, one brings upon oneself all the sins and transgressions of those whose faults one has sought and whose evils one has spoken. This is what is called slander (*apavādī*). Thus says the *Dharmaśāstra*: "It is a constant [sin]."
From the forehead the Brahmin is born, and likewise the Kṣatriya from the arms;
from the thighs the Vaiśya is born, and the Śūdra is likewise born from the feet.

[Regarding the Kaliṅga: Now, as for what is called "birth," it originated from the body of the venerable Lord Brahmā previously mentioned. He established what are known as the four castes (*caturvarṇa*) in the world. The one called *vipra* is the Brāhmaṇa. He arose from the forehead of Lord Brahmā. His duties are: to perform worship, to offer oblations (*homa*), to perform sacrifices (*yajña*), to recite mantras, to practice yoga and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and to understand all the scriptures (*sarvaśāstra*). He is the locus of the four Vedas; he is the distinguished caste.

The one called a Kṣatriya is a king who was born from the arm of the venerable Brahmā. His duty is to know warfare and all the *śāstras*; he must be skilled in archery and endowed with royal splendor (*śrī*). He is courageous in the kingdom, maintains discernment toward the Brāhmaṇas in his duties, and bestows gifts. He protects the realm; he is brave yet possesses foresight, remains steadfast in his affection, avoids the wicked, and is a refuge for the virtuous.

Who is this Vaiśya? A person of that birth, born from the seed of the venerable Brahmā; his function is to protect the earth, to cause it to flourish and prosper, to cultivate and tend to all seeds, and to provide sustenance for the kingdom; he is the one served by the Kṣatriya.

Next is the Śūdra, whose occupation is trade. He is born from the foot of the venerable Brahmā; his business is buying and selling. Buying and selling means bartering goods, both small and large, exchanging items, and trading. He fashions ornaments and is made a servant by the Kṣatriya. Such are the distinctions of the duties of the four castes. As for the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, they all show devotion toward the Brāhmaṇa, who is regarded by the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra as their spiritual teacher (*guru*) in terms of essential truth. However, when they do not adhere to his proper order, moving about hither and thither, that is called the "world turning upside down" (*jagat-harohara*). It is neither low nor high; it is called "upside down" (*acarub*), meaning it is neither low nor high. That is the sign of the dissolution of the world (*rātsaṅhāra*). When the world has thus turned back, there will be no distinction between kin, caste, or lineage, nor even between morning and evening.
Even now, O father, consider this: transgressing against one who is called *atuhatuha* and a teacher, he has been punished along with his children and his mother-in-law.

Even though one may be a son of Bappa Pinakaśatru, possessing great power, wealth, and honor, with a body that does not age, a life that does not decay, and a complexion that never fades, even if one is surrounded by many auspicious attendants—because the kingdom is not yet established, lacking a father, lacking a grandfather, lacking elders, and lacking those who can provide counsel—there exists a Brāhmaṇa who is wise, a Śaiva, Sogata, or Ṛṣi who is learned and provides counsel based on reason and logic, whose speech is consistent with his own nature, whose mind is always alert, and whose intellect is clear. Just as a skilled charioteer guides a horse, so too is a noble person guided by reason regarding what is right and wrong. Just as the water of the ocean is its very essence and the lotus is its very flower, such is the nature of man in the Kali Yuga: birth is his essence, and his conduct is his flower. His manifestation is his counsel, which is expressed and practiced through noble deeds; it is that which must be sought and understood. Therefore, one who knows this should not be led astray by the intellect of men in the Kali Yuga.
One question is for the sake of debate; one is for the support of the foolish;
one is for the purpose of examining another; and one is for the sake of humiliation.

[On] the types of questions (*kaliṅanya*): a question is that which is asked by a person. There is a question made for the sake of inquiry; there is a question made for the sake of testing, as in the case of the testing of a gem; there is a question made for the sake of examination, desiring to discern the nature and quality of what is being questioned; and there is a question made for the sake of refuting what has been stated. Such are the fourfold divisions. [The four purposes are: for the sake of dispute (*vivādārtha*), [for the sake of knowledge, for the sake of examination, and] for the sake of humiliation (*paribhavārtha*). These are the four types of questions. Whatever constitutes the substance of a question, it should be understood in this very same way by a wise man (*vidagdha-puruṣa*).
Just as gold is tested by four means—
by rubbing, by striking, by cutting, and by heating—
so too is a person tested by four means.
[Verse 80d] By means of learning, ethical conduct, virtue, and action.

[Kaliṅganyā] Regarding that, one should observe the immortals (the gods). Listen to their sequence: *nigharṣaṇa* means rubbing without cause; *tāḍana* means striking without cause; *chedana* means cutting without cause; *tāpana* means burning without cause. Such is the observation of the immortals.

How does one examine a person? That which is known through reflection is not understood by birth alone; rather, it is through examination that one comes to know their lineage and nature. The methods of examination are as follows: by means of learning (*śruta*), one understands the cause of their majesty; by means of conduct (*śīla*), one understands whether their character is virtuous or lacking in virtue; by means of qualities (*guṇa*), one understands the excellence of their wisdom; and by means of action (*karman*), one understands the nature of their deeds. What has been described here is how one may discern the lineage of a person. Thus, one observes whether a person is of noble birth or not by their appearance and gestures.
Conduct reveals one's family; speech reveals one's country;
the heart reveals one's eyes; and the body reveals one's food.

[Sloka 81j] Regarding Kaliṅga: conduct reflects the lineage of a person; speech reflects the customs of the person's native land; the eyes reflect the inner purity or impurity of the person's heart; and the body reflects whether one's enjoyment is like that of a deer or abundant in enjoyment. Such is the reflection of a person's behavior.
By means of physical forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face, one who has been examined becomes known.

[Regarding] the Kaliṅga: one should examine the person who desires immortality through the signs (*liṅga*) of birth. There are nine types of these. They are as follows: *ākāra* means the observation of the configuration of their form; *iṅgita* means observing their smiles and gestures; *gati* means observing their manner of walking; *ceṣṭā* means observing the movements of their limbs—these are the first four. *Bhāṣita* means paying attention to their speech; this is the fifth. Furthermore, there is finally the observation of the face and eyes, if there is a change in their appearance. "Change" (*vikāra*) means that a certain expression is seen on the face and eyes, for the wicked and the virtuous are different. There are many varieties of them. The type of the wicked person’s expression is one that conceals its true intent with the mouth, because it conceals its inner mind, since their heart is full of malice. Such is the examination of a person who is difficult to influence toward evil. However, the virtuous person manifests a gentle, peaceful, and serene disposition in their appearance, because the depths of their heart cannot be influenced by evil; they are simply pure at all times. Such is the sequence stated in the Holy Scripture (*śāstra*).
Even when fallen into adversity, one who recognizes faults should not abandon the treatises on Dharma;
just as a bee does not leave a lotus, even if its petals are torn by its own kin.

[Verse 83j] Regarding Kaliṅga: "The wise man is one who knows faults. This means that even when he has fallen into misfortune—having been harmed by the wicked—the wise man does not lose his adherence to *dharma* and the traditional scriptures (*śāstrāgama*), nor does he cease from virtuous conduct. This is because it is the very nature (*svajāti*) of the wise man, just like the *bhṛṅga*. *Bhṛṅga* here refers to the bee. Even though its wings are clipped and it is unable to fly, the bee does not lose its longing for the lotus flower; it still desires to sip its nectar, even if it must defecate while doing so. It is not otherwise. So it is with the wise man: even if he should happen to commit some slight transgression, or if he is harmed by wicked people, he does not become habitually inclined toward evil in this world. Even if he suffers many afflictions and is beset by the wicked, he does not repeatedly harbor malice toward the world.
[Verse 84] Ten ultimate realities, ten impurities, nine attachments.

[Śloka 84j §1] Now, these are the ten supreme goals (*daśa paramārtha*). One should practice them; they are the qualities of a servant. One should abandon all forms of non-restraint (*avirati*). One who desires to attain the human birth—having escaped from the depths of evil—should indeed perform these ten supreme goals. They are as follows: austerity (*tapa*), observance (*vrata*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), tranquility (*śānta*), right view (*sanmata*), compassion (*karuṇā*), kindness (*karuṇi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Their sequence is as follows: austerity is the abandonment of non-restraint. Observance is the withdrawal from all objects of sensual pleasure. Meditative concentration is the repeated practice of directing the mind inward toward the Divine Dharma. Tranquility is the state of being a single sound, without distraction. Right view is being singularly intent upon the welfare of living beings alone, without concern for one's own body. Compassion is not being weary of the suffering of living beings. Kindness is the love for all that grows, extending to every single creature. Equanimity is knowing the difference between the harmful and the beneficial, so as not to harm the deluded person who comes seeking refuge. Sympathetic joy is the delight in the excellence of the intellect, which does not waver even when it is spoken of. Loving-kindness is the utterance of auspicious sounds toward all fellow living beings.

[Chapter 84: The Ten Defilements] I shall now explain the ten defilements (*daśa-mala*), which are unfit for one’s conduct. Their forms are: indolence (*tandrī*), sloth (*kleda*), shamelessness (*laja*), hypocrisy (*kuhaka*), arrogance (*metraya*), pride (*magata*), lust for women (*rāga-strī*), crookedness (*kuṭila*), gluttony (*bhakṣa-bhuvana*), and greed (*kimburu*). Indolence is when a person is lazy, sluggish, and lacking in vigor; though they may appear outwardly auspicious, their inner intent is actually evil. Sloth is when one is indolent and lethargic, wallowing in desire, and unable to distinguish between what is beneficial and what is not. Shamelessness is when one is overcome by passion, possessing great thirst and great attachment toward evil. Crookedness is when one seeks out the faults of others, being full of suspicion regarding the lapses in others' affection, negligent and fickle, and stealing the wealth of people through deception. Hypocrisy is when one is overcome by anger, possessing great malice, using harsh words, and being deceitful. Arrogance is when one speaks with excessive pride, acts with ostentation, lacks discernment and discrimination, and is like a person who has lost his way in the middle of a vast desert at night—his conduct is never auspicious. Even if his speech grows sweet and pleasing, within him there is only evil; his intellect is not refined, and he does not purify the time spent in his heart. Lust for women is when one is greatly obsessed with women, with eyes that wander restlessly. Gluttony is when one eats and drinks excessively, behaving improperly toward virtuous people, making loud and coarse noises while eating and drinking. Greed is when one seeks out improper things, coveting the wealth of virtuous people, kin, and friends, and being so attached that one even steals from the ascetics (*saṅ viku*). Such is the sequence of the ten defilements; they are not auspicious.

[Verse 84j §3] Here are the nine qualities of one who has attained the auspicious state of perfection (*siddha-rahayu*). Their types are: *andrayuga*, *guṇabhikṣama*, *sādhuniragṛha*, *vidagdhaprasanna*, *virotasādhāraṇa*, *kṛtarājahita*, *tyāgaprasanna*, *śūralakṣaṇa*, and *śūrapratyayana*. These are their characteristics: *Andrayuga*: He possesses the wisdom that follows the Dharma; he is capable of performing his duties. *Guṇabhikṣama*: He is virtuous regarding the purpose of the Lord; he is diligent in his tasks; he maintains equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward those who oppose him; he is obedient to many people; he finds it easy to perform what is good. *Sādhuniragṛha*: He is virtuous in his speech; he does not hesitate when dealing with his equals. *Vidagdhaprasanna*: He does not consume improper sounds in his presence; he does not listen to slander; his clear intellect is excellent. *Virotasādhāraṇa*: His speech is not untruthful; he is not indignant at words; he takes pleasure in statesmanship (*nīti*). *Kṛtarājahita*: He is not indignant; he knows the *Kuṭāramānavāda* (the science of weaponry). *T्यāgaprasanna*: He does not find it difficult when sent by the Lord. *Śūralakṣaṇa*: He does not shrink from battle; he stands firm and does not flee. *Śūrapratyayana*: He is devoted to the Lord; he is courageous in combat; he is diligent in his tasks; he protects the Lord. These are the nine qualities.
